title: Italian grammar A1: first useful sentences

sources.title: Council of Europe, CEFR Companion Volume (2020), communicative competence descriptors
Treccani, Indicativo passato prossimo (La grammatica italiana)

units.title: First sentences and readable words
units.description: Build a simple Italian sentence and recognize spelling cues that affect meaning.

lessons.title: Read key letter patterns
lessons.outcome: I can read common c, g, ch, gh, and sc spellings in familiar words.
lessons.takeaway: The next letter changes the sound of c and g; h keeps a hard sound before e or i.

objectives.label: Read key letter patterns
objectives.explanation: The next letter changes the sound of c and g; h keeps a hard sound before e or i.

teach.title: Soft and hard c
teach.body: Before e or i, c is soft as in cena; before a, o or u it is hard as in casa. Add h to keep c hard before e or i.

examples.en: Chiara is looking for a house.

teach.title: The same cue with g and sc
teach.body: Gi gives a soft g; gh before e or i gives a hard g. Sc before e or i is the sound in scena; sch keeps a hard sc.
teach.tip: These spelling cues help you read, but natural stress still needs practice.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: C before e gives the soft sound in cena.
questions.hint: Think of the Italian word for dinner.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: Anna buys a kilo of bread.
questions.explanation: Ch before i keeps the hard k sound.
questions.hint: A hard c before i needs h.
questions.speak: Anna compra un chilo di pane.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.explanation: Ge gives the soft g in gelato.
questions.hint: Begin with the article and noun.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.explanation: Gh before e keeps the hard g sound.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.context: Nel film, la ___ finale è bella.
questions.translation: In the film, the final scene is beautiful.
questions.explanation: Sc before e gives the sound in scena.
questions.hint: The scene is spelled with sc before e.
questions.speak: Nel film, la scena finale è bella.

lessons.title: Say who and what
lessons.outcome: I can make a basic subject–verb–complement sentence and omit a clear subject pronoun.
lessons.takeaway: Italian usually puts the finite verb after the subject, and its ending often identifies the subject.

objectives.label: Say who and what
objectives.explanation: Italian usually puts the finite verb after the subject, and its ending often identifies the subject.

teach.title: A first sentence
teach.body: A simple statement can be subject + verb + complement. Keep the subject when it clarifies who you mean.

teach.title: The subject can be understood
teach.body: Italian commonly leaves out io or tu when the verb ending already tells us who acts.
teach.tip: Include io for emphasis or contrast: Io parlo italiano, lui no.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: Maria is the subject and comes before parla.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: Vivo already means “I live”; io is optional.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.explanation: The subject Luca comes before beve and its object.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.explanation: Parlo is the first-person present of parlare.

lessons.title: Say who you are
lessons.outcome: I can use present forms of essere for identity and origin.
lessons.takeaway: Sono, sei, è, siamo, siete, sono change with the subject.

objectives.label: Say who you are
objectives.explanation: Sono, sei, è, siamo, siete, sono change with the subject.

teach.title: Singular forms
teach.body: Use sono for I, sei for informal you, and è for he, she, or a named singular person.

examples.it: Sono Anna e sono di Milano.
examples.en: I am Anna and I am from Milan.

teach.title: Plural forms
teach.body: Use siamo for we, siete for you plural, and sono for they. Keep the accent in è.
teach.tip: Italian normally has no indefinite article before an unmodified profession: Sono medico.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: Tu takes sei, not sono or è.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: È is the verb “is”; e without the accent means “and”.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.explanation: Siamo is the we form of essere.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.explanation: Voi takes siete.

lessons.title: Say what you have
lessons.outcome: I can use avere for possession, age, and hunger.
lessons.takeaway: Italian uses avere for possession and several states that use “be” in English.

objectives.label: Say what you have
objectives.explanation: Italian uses avere for possession and several states that use “be” in English.

teach.title: Possession and age
teach.body: Ho, hai, ha, abbiamo, avete, hanno are present forms of avere. Age uses avere + number + anni.

teach.title: Everyday states
teach.body: Say avere fame, sete, caldo, freddo, or paura. The h in ho, hai, ha, hanno is written but silent.

examples.en: We are hungry after the journey.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: Io takes ho.
questions.hint: The h is silent but written.

questions.prompt: Match the Italian sentence halves.
questions.explanation: Each subject takes its own form of avere; age and physical states use avere in Italian.
questions.hint: Match the person to ho, hai, or ha.
questions.speak: Io ho fame dopo il viaggio.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.explanation: Abbiamo fame means “we are hungry.”
questions.hint: Start with the we form of avere.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.explanation: Voi takes avete; sete is “thirst.”
questions.hint: Use the plural you form of avere.

units.title: Nouns and agreement
units.description: Choose noun forms, articles, and adjectives that belong together.

lessons.title: Recognize noun gender
lessons.outcome: I can use a noun ending and its article as clues to gender.
lessons.takeaway: Most -o nouns are masculine and most -a nouns feminine; learn -e nouns with their article.

objectives.label: Recognize noun gender
objectives.explanation: Most -o nouns are masculine and most -a nouns feminine; learn -e nouns with their article.

teach.title: Useful endings
teach.body: Most singular nouns in -o are masculine and most in -a are feminine. The article confirms the gender.

examples.en: The book is on the table.

teach.title: Learn -e with the article
teach.body: An -e noun may be masculine or feminine: il pane, la notte. Endings are clues rather than guarantees.
teach.tip: La mano is a frequent feminine exception to the -o pattern.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: Casa is feminine, so use la.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: Pane ends in -e but is masculine; learn it with il.
questions.hint: Do not infer gender from -e alone.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.explanation: Mano is a feminine exception, so la and fredda agree.
questions.hint: The article for mano is la.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.explanation: Libro is masculine singular.
questions.hint: Use the basic masculine singular article.

lessons.title: Introduce one thing
lessons.outcome: I can choose un, uno, una, or un’ in a new-item phrase.
lessons.takeaway: The indefinite article follows gender and the next sound; masculine un has no apostrophe.

objectives.label: Introduce one thing
objectives.explanation: The indefinite article follows gender and the next sound; masculine un has no apostrophe.

teach.title: Un and una
teach.body: Use un before most masculine nouns, even a vowel: un amico. Use una before a feminine consonant: una casa.

examples.en: I have a friend in Rome.

teach.title: Special beginnings
teach.body: Use uno before masculine s + consonant or z. Before a feminine vowel, una shortens to un’ with an apostrophe.

examples.en: Anna is a friend of Luca.

teach.tip: An apostrophe after un signals a feminine noun.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: I am looking for one male student for the project.
questions.explanation: Studente begins with s + consonant, so masculine uno is required.
questions.hint: Look at the start of studente.
questions.speak: Cerco uno studente per il progetto.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: I have a female friend in Florence.
questions.explanation: Before feminine amica, una becomes un’.
questions.hint: The friend is female and the noun begins with a vowel.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.explanation: Masculine amico takes un without an apostrophe.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.translation: I am buying a small house.
questions.explanation: Casa is feminine and begins with a consonant.
questions.hint: Use the full feminine singular form.

lessons.title: Name known things
lessons.outcome: I can choose singular and plural definite articles, including lo and gli.
lessons.takeaway: Articles agree with the noun, and lo/gli appear before certain masculine beginnings.

objectives.label: Name known things
objectives.explanation: Articles agree with the noun, and lo/gli appear before certain masculine beginnings.

teach.title: Basic article pairs
teach.body: Il becomes i; la becomes le. Before a vowel, singular il or la becomes l’.

examples.en: The girl is reading the book.

teach.title: Lo and gli
teach.body: Use lo before masculine s + consonant or z, and gli for its plural; gli also stands before masculine plural vowels.

examples.en: The students are waiting for the train.

teach.tip: L’ before a vowel hides gender; check the noun or plural.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: The masculine plural of lo studente is gli studenti.

questions.prompt: Match the Italian sentence halves.
questions.explanation: Il, lo, and le each fit a different noun by gender, number, and initial sound.
questions.hint: Check the first sound and whether the noun is plural.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.explanation: Zaino begins with z, so use lo.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.translation: The books are on the table.
questions.explanation: Libri is masculine plural and begins with an ordinary consonant.

lessons.title: Make common plurals
lessons.outcome: I can form regular noun plurals and keep the article in agreement.
lessons.takeaway: Regular -o/-e nouns usually take -i; regular feminine -a nouns take -e.

objectives.label: Make common plurals
objectives.explanation: Regular -o/-e nouns usually take -i; regular feminine -a nouns take -e.

teach.title: The common changes
teach.body: Il libro becomes i libri; la casa becomes le case. Many nouns ending -e take -i, whatever their gender.

teach.title: Spelling protects the sound
teach.body: C or g before -a often needs h in the plural to keep the hard sound: amica → amiche. Some nouns, such as città, do not change.
teach.tip: Learn irregular or invariable plurals with each noun.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: Libro changes -o to -i in the plural.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: Amica changes -ca to -che to keep the hard c sound.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.explanation: Città has the same written form in singular and plural.
questions.hint: The plural article reveals the number.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.context: Ci sono tre ___ vicino alla stazione.
questions.translation: There are three houses near the station.
questions.explanation: Casa changes -a to -e in the plural.
questions.speak: Ci sono tre case vicino alla stazione.

lessons.title: Describe a noun
lessons.outcome: I can make a common adjective agree in gender and number.
lessons.takeaway: An adjective normally changes with the noun it describes, whether before or after it.

objectives.label: Describe a noun
objectives.explanation: An adjective normally changes with the noun it describes, whether before or after it.

teach.title: Four endings
teach.body: A four-form adjective such as piccolo has piccola, piccoli, piccole. Match the noun’s gender and number.

teach.title: Two-form adjectives
teach.body: Grande has grande in both singular genders and grandi in both plurals. Agreement still matters.
teach.tip: The form describes the noun, not the speaker.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: Ragazze is feminine plural; stanche agrees with it.
questions.hint: Look at both gender and number.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: Tavolo is masculine singular.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.explanation: Grande changes to grandi for a plural noun.
questions.hint: End the sentence with the plural adjective.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.explanation: Ragazzi is masculine plural, so contento becomes contenti.

units.title: Present time
units.description: Speak about routines, ask simple questions, and say what is present.

lessons.title: Use -are verbs now
lessons.outcome: I can conjugate regular -are verbs for everyday present actions.
lessons.takeaway: Take off -are and add -o, -i, -a, -iamo, -ate, -ano.

objectives.label: Use -are verbs now
objectives.explanation: Take off -are and add -o, -i, -a, -iamo, -ate, -ano.

teach.title: Singular -are
teach.body: Parlare becomes parlo, parli, parla. The ending usually tells who is acting.

examples.en: Today I am speaking with Anna.

teach.title: Plural -are
teach.body: Parliamo, parlate, parlano are the we, you-plural, and they forms. The present can describe a habit or an action now.
teach.tip: Some verbs retain a hard c/g spelling with h, as in cerchiamo.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: Noi takes the -iamo ending.

questions.prompt: Match the Italian sentence halves.
questions.explanation: The regular -are ending changes with io, noi, and loro.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: You all speak with the teacher.
questions.explanation: Parlate is the voi form.
questions.hint: Start with the verb for you all.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.explanation: Io takes -o with a regular -are verb.
questions.hint: Use lavorare with the I ending.

lessons.title: Use -ere verbs now
lessons.outcome: I can use regular -ere endings in short present sentences.
lessons.takeaway: A regular -ere verb takes -o, -i, -e, -iamo, -ete, -ono.

objectives.label: Use -ere verbs now
objectives.explanation: A regular -ere verb takes -o, -i, -e, -iamo, -ete, -ono.

teach.title: Singular -ere
teach.body: Vivere gives vivo, vivi, vive. Match the ending to the person.

teach.title: Plural -ere
teach.body: Viviamo, vivete, vivono cover we, you-plural, and they. Many -ere verbs have irregular stems; learn those separately.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: Do you live near the school?
questions.explanation: Tu takes -i in the present.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: You all take the train at eight.
questions.explanation: Voi takes -ete with prendere.
questions.speak: Voi prendete il treno alle otto.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.explanation: Vivono ends in -ono for loro.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.explanation: Noi takes -iamo.
questions.hint: Use prendere with the we ending.

lessons.title: Use -ire verbs now
lessons.outcome: I can distinguish a plain -ire present from a common -isc- pattern.
lessons.takeaway: Dormire uses dormo/dormi/dorme; capire inserts -isc- except with noi and voi.

objectives.label: Use -ire verbs now
objectives.explanation: Dormire uses dormo/dormi/dorme; capire inserts -isc- except with noi and voi.

teach.title: Plain -ire
teach.body: Dormire gives dormo, dormi, dorme, dormiamo, dormite, dormono.

teach.title: The -isc- family
teach.body: Capire gives capisco, capisci, capisce, capiamo, capite, capiscono. The -isc- element is absent in noi and voi.
teach.tip: Learn which -ire verbs belong to this family.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: Capire adds -isc- in the io form.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: Noi omits -isc-: finiamo.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: Marta is sleeping on the sofa.
questions.explanation: Dormire is a plain -ire verb: Marta dorme.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.explanation: Loro takes capiscono with -isc-.
questions.hint: The third-person plural -isc- form ends in -ono.

lessons.title: Use common irregular presents
lessons.outcome: I can use fare and andare for simple actions and destinations.
lessons.takeaway: High-frequency verbs such as fare and andare have forms to learn as whole words.

objectives.label: Use common irregular presents
objectives.explanation: High-frequency verbs such as fare and andare have forms to learn as whole words.

teach.title: Fare
teach.body: Fare has faccio, fai, fa, facciamo, fate, fanno. Use it for doing or making.

teach.title: Andare
teach.body: Andare has vado, vai, va, andiamo, andate, vanno. With a city, use a: vado a Roma.

examples.en: Tomorrow we are going to Naples.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: I am doing the shopping today.
questions.explanation: The io form of fare is faccio.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: Luca goes to school by bus.
questions.explanation: Luca takes the third-person form va.
questions.speak: Luca va a scuola in autobus.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: We are going to the cinema tonight.
questions.explanation: Andiamo is the noi form.
questions.hint: Start with the we form of andare.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.explanation: Voi takes fate, not a regular -are form.
questions.hint: The plural you form is short.

lessons.title: Ask and negate
lessons.outcome: I can ask a yes–no or question-word question and place non before a verb.
lessons.takeaway: A yes–no question can keep statement order; non goes directly before the finite verb.

objectives.label: Ask and negate
objectives.explanation: A yes–no question can keep statement order; non goes directly before the finite verb.

teach.title: Ask without do
teach.body: Italian can use ordinary statement order with question intonation and a question mark. Question words such as dove come first.

teach.title: Negate the verb
teach.body: Put non immediately before the conjugated verb, including an auxiliary.
teach.tip: Do not add a separate Italian equivalent of English do.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: Dove asks for a place.
questions.hint: The answer would be a place.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: Non goes before mangio.
questions.hint: Use the basic negator before the verb.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.explanation: A yes–no question needs no extra do verb.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.explanation: Non stands directly before parla.
questions.hint: Put the negative before the verb.

lessons.title: Say what is there
lessons.outcome: I can distinguish c’è from ci sono for one or several things.
lessons.takeaway: C’è introduces a singular thing; ci sono introduces plural things.

objectives.label: Say what is there
objectives.explanation: C’è introduces a singular thing; ci sono introduces plural things.

teach.title: One thing
teach.body: Use c’è with a singular noun or a mass noun: c’è una farmacia, c’è acqua.

examples.it: C’è una farmacia vicino a casa.
examples.en: There is a pharmacy near home.

teach.title: Several things
teach.body: Use ci sono with plural nouns. In a question, keep the same form and add question intonation.

examples.it: Ci sono due sedie in cucina.
examples.en: There are two chairs in the kitchen.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: There are two books on the table.
questions.explanation: Due libri is plural, so use ci sono.
questions.speak: Ci sono due libri sul tavolo.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: Is there a station near here?
questions.explanation: Una stazione is singular; a question still uses c’è.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.explanation: Ci sono stays together before a plural noun.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.translation: There is milk in the fridge.
questions.explanation: Latte is a mass noun here, so use singular c’è.
questions.hint: Treat the milk as one amount.

units.title: Describe and locate
units.description: Say whose thing it is, point to it, and place it in everyday space and time.

lessons.title: Say whose it is
lessons.outcome: I can use basic possessive adjectives with the article.
lessons.takeaway: The possessive agrees with the thing owned, not its owner; a singular close family member often omits the article.

objectives.label: Say whose it is
objectives.explanation: The possessive agrees with the thing owned, not its owner; a singular close family member often omits the article.

teach.title: Agree with the thing
teach.body: Say il mio libro, la mia casa, i miei libri, le mie case. The noun controls the ending.

teach.title: The family shortcut
teach.body: With a singular close family member, normally omit the article: mia madre, tuo fratello. Keep it with plurals: i miei fratelli.
teach.tip: Formal or modified family phrases can differ; start with this common pattern.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: Libro is masculine singular, so il mio agrees with it.

questions.prompt: Match the Italian sentence halves.
questions.explanation: A singular close family term normally has no article; other possessives agree with the noun.
questions.hint: Match the noun’s number and gender.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.explanation: Amiche is feminine plural, so le mie agrees.
questions.hint: Begin with the feminine plural article.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.explanation: Chiavi is feminine plural, so use le tue.
questions.hint: Agree with the plural keys, not their owner.

lessons.title: Point to this or that
lessons.outcome: I can use common questo and quello forms with a nearby or distant noun.
lessons.takeaway: Questo agrees like an adjective; quello follows the article pattern before a noun.

objectives.label: Point to this or that
objectives.explanation: Questo agrees like an adjective; quello follows the article pattern before a noun.

teach.title: Nearby: questo
teach.body: Questo, questa, questi, queste agree with the noun. Use them for something near in space or in the conversation.

teach.title: Farther away: quello
teach.body: Before a noun, use quel libro, quello studente, quella casa; plural forms include quei libri and quegli studenti.
teach.tip: The form before a noun follows the same sound pattern as il/lo/gli.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: This girl here is my sister.
questions.explanation: Ragazza is feminine singular and is here, so questa.
questions.hint: Use feminine singular for someone nearby.
questions.speak: Questa ragazza qui è mia sorella.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: That student over there is Marco.
questions.explanation: Before masculine studente (s + consonant), use quello.
questions.hint: This start works like lo studente.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.explanation: Questi agrees with masculine plural libri.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.translation: That house over there is big.
questions.explanation: Casa is feminine singular, so use quella.
questions.hint: Use the feminine form for a distant house.

lessons.title: Choose a basic preposition
lessons.outcome: I can use a, in, da, and con in common place and company phrases.
lessons.takeaway: Learn frequent preposition patterns with the verb and destination.

objectives.label: Choose a basic preposition
objectives.explanation: Learn frequent preposition patterns with the verb and destination.

teach.title: To a city; in a country
teach.body: Use a with most city names and in with most countries or regions: a Roma, in Italia.

examples.en: I am going to Rome tomorrow.

teach.title: From or with
teach.body: Da marks origin or going to a person; con means with. These are different relationships.

examples.en: I come from Milan with Luca.

teach.tip: Prepositions are best learned with whole phrases.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: Tomorrow we are going to Florence.
questions.explanation: Most city destinations take a.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: Da marks her place of origin.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.explanation: A country name commonly takes in.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.translation: I am going out with my sister.
questions.explanation: Con indicates company.

lessons.title: Combine a preposition and article
lessons.outcome: I can form frequent a + article and in + article combinations.
lessons.takeaway: When a or in meets a definite article, they normally join in writing.

objectives.label: Combine a preposition and article
objectives.explanation: When a or in meets a definite article, they normally join in writing.

teach.title: A + article
teach.body: A + il becomes al; a + la becomes alla; a + lo becomes allo. Use these for a definite place or person.

examples.en: I am going to the market.

teach.title: In + article
teach.body: In + il becomes nel, in + lo becomes nello, and in + la becomes nella; plural forms include nei and nelle.

examples.en: The milk is in the fridge.

teach.tip: A bare place expression can differ: a scuola, in centro.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: I am going to the cinema tonight.
questions.explanation: A + il cinema becomes al cinema.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: The keys are in the bag.
questions.explanation: In + la borsa becomes nella borsa.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.explanation: A + la stazione becomes alla stazione.
questions.hint: Use the fused form before stazione.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.translation: The books are in the backpack.
questions.explanation: In + lo zaino becomes nello zaino.
questions.hint: Zaino takes lo; combine in with lo.

lessons.title: Say how much and when
lessons.outcome: I can use basic quantities and clock-time phrases in daily plans.
lessons.takeaway: A quantity word describes amount; alle introduces a clock time other than one o’clock.

objectives.label: Say how much and when
objectives.explanation: A quantity word describes amount; alle introduces a clock time other than one o’clock.

teach.title: Amount in a noun phrase
teach.body: Molto and poco can agree with a countable noun: molti libri, poche mele. With a mass noun, use singular: molta acqua.

teach.title: Clock times
teach.body: Say alle otto, alle nove, but all’una. Put the time after the event in a simple plan.
teach.tip: A day word such as domani needs no preposition: parto domani.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: A plural clock hour uses alle.

units.title: Daily interaction
units.description: Ask for help, give a simple instruction, express a preference, and mention yesterday.

lessons.title: Ask to do something
lessons.outcome: I can use posso, vuoi, and devo before an infinitive in short requests.
lessons.takeaway: A modal verb carries person; the following action stays in the infinitive.

objectives.label: Ask to do something
objectives.explanation: A modal verb carries person; the following action stays in the infinitive.

teach.title: Permission and offers
teach.body: Posso + infinitive asks if I may do something; vuoi + infinitive asks if someone wants to.

teach.title: Need or obligation
teach.body: Devo + infinitive says I need to do something. Add per favore to a direct request when appropriate.

examples.en: I need to call my mother.

teach.tip: The second verb remains aprire, chiamare, or another infinitive.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: Posso is the io form for asking my own permission.
questions.hint: Ask about what I may do.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: Do you want to drink something?
questions.explanation: Tu takes vuoi; bere remains an infinitive.
questions.hint: Use the tu form of volere.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.explanation: After devo the action stays in the infinitive comprare.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.translation: Can you call a taxi, please?
questions.explanation: The informal tu form is puoi, followed by chiamare.
questions.speak: Puoi chiamare un taxi, per favore?

lessons.title: Give a simple tu instruction
lessons.outcome: I can use common affirmative tu commands in familiar situations.
lessons.takeaway: For regular tu commands, -are has -a and -ere/-ire usually have -i.

objectives.label: Give a simple tu instruction
objectives.explanation: For regular tu commands, -are has -a and -ere/-ire usually have -i.

teach.title: Regular tu commands
teach.body: Parla!, Prendi!, Dormi! address one person informally. A command can sound warmer with per favore.

teach.title: Everyday irregulars
teach.body: Some frequent commands must be learned: vai/va’, fai/fa’, dai/da’, stai/sta’. Use the familiar form with someone you call tu.
teach.tip: Polite formal requests use another form, taught later.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: Chiudi is the tu command of chiudere.
questions.hint: Address one person you call tu.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: A regular -are tu command ends in -a.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.explanation: Prendi directly addresses one familiar person.

questions.prompt: Match the Italian sentence halves.
questions.explanation: Each tu command combines with an object or manner that makes a natural instruction.
questions.hint: Match the action to what can follow it.

lessons.title: Say what you like
lessons.outcome: I can use mi piace with one thing and mi piacciono with several.
lessons.takeaway: The thing liked controls the verb: piace for singular, piacciono for plural.

objectives.label: Say what you like
objectives.explanation: The thing liked controls the verb: piace for singular, piacciono for plural.

teach.title: One thing or activity
teach.body: Mi piace + a singular noun or an infinitive means I like it. The grammatical subject is the thing liked.

teach.title: Several things
teach.body: Mi piacciono + plural noun. Ti gives “you like” with the same singular/plural verb choice.
teach.tip: Do not use English-like “I like” word order with piacere.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: Pizza is singular, so use piace.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: Film italiani is plural, so use piacciono.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: I like reading in the evening.
questions.explanation: An infinitive activity uses piace.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.explanation: Queste canzoni is plural, so the verb is piacciono.

lessons.title: Report one completed event
lessons.outcome: I can use a familiar avere + participle phrase for something that happened yesterday.
lessons.takeaway: Ho/hai/ha + a regular past participle reports a completed event.

objectives.label: Report one completed event
objectives.explanation: Ho/hai/ha + a regular past participle reports a completed event.

teach.title: A first past phrase
teach.body: Use present avere plus a past participle: ho mangiato, hai parlato, ha comprato.

teach.title: Make the participle
teach.body: Regular -are changes to -ato, -ere to -uto, and -ire to -ito. Keep the participle after the auxiliary.
teach.tip: A2 expands this pattern with essere and irregular participles.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.explanation: Mangiare takes avere in the passato prossimo: ho mangiato.
questions.speak: Ieri io ho mangiato la pizza.

questions.prompt: Choose the form that completes the sentence.
questions.translation: On Saturday Marta bought a book.
questions.explanation: Marta takes ha plus comprato for a completed purchase.
questions.speak: Sabato Marta ha comprato un libro.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to say this in Italian.
questions.translation: Yesterday we talked for a long time.
questions.explanation: Abbiamo + parlato marks one completed past conversation.

questions.prompt: Type the missing Italian word or short phrase.
questions.explanation: Dormire forms the regular participle dormito and uses avere.
questions.speak: Ieri tu hai dormito fino alle nove.
